name: project-tinygl-pipes-spike
description: "State of the TinyGL-on-the-S3 spike for porting Pipes (first GL hack): decisions, corrections, where the throwaway code lives"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 677be71b-6b3b-46bc-98ff-f004e6cfc668

Rod chose Pipes as the first GL hack, TinyGL (C-Chads fork, commit 36a7987) as the rasteriser, "Pipes first, grow later" for scope, and a device speed spike before any spec (2026-10-09). Brainstorming path: architectural, so spec then plan; the spike is the de-risking step.

Facts learned:

- TinyGL's licence is zlib-style, not MIT, and clause 1 requires an acknowledgment in the product and its documentation. Needs a `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` row and README credit if kept.
- Pipes (6.16) does NOT accumulate: every frame it `glClear`s and redraws every piece so far (up to about 500 per system, 5 systems, default) from display lists under a slowly rotating camera. Cost scales with piece count and every frame is a full-frame change. I first told Rod the opposite; that was wrong.
- Pipes needs `sphere.c`, `buildlwo.c`, `teapot.c`, `gltrackball.c`, `rotator.c`, `xlock-gl-utils.c` from `hacks/glx/` (byte-identical copies are allowed there; only `utils/` is off limits).
- Canvas pixels are byte-swapped RGB565 and rows need `canvas_mark_dirty`; the spike swaps and marks on copy.
- Spike code is committed (fe66810) and pushed to `origin/worktree-spike-tinygl`, no PR. It is `firmware/src/hacks/tglspike.c` (top level, because `check_notices.py` treats files in `hacks/<subdir>/` as third-party), envs `spike` and `spike_dump`, guarded by `-DTGL_SPIKE`. The TinyGL copy (`firmware/spike_tinygl/`) is untracked; `firmware/spike_tinygl.patch` rebuilds it from upstream 36a7987 and `docs/tinygl-spike.md` has the steps. Throwaway.
- GL hack survey (146 GL hacks; 87 use textures, 84 blending, 17 fog; only 36 clean of textures/blend/fog/stencil/readback). TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays`. Flying Toasters needs all three plus two PNG textures (about 10k lit vertices per frame at the default 20 floaters: bounded, unlike Pipes). Candidate first GL hacks are estimates, not measured: gears, morph3d, stonerview, kallisti.
- Upstream TinyGL quirks fixed in the private copy: `memory.c` tests `TGL_FEATURE_CUSTOM_MALLOC` before including its header; `memset_s` clashes with macOS `string.h`.

Device results (2026-10-09, 464x464 16-bit, z-buffer and framebuffer in PSRAM, S3):

- TinyGL display lists cost a 16 KB op buffer each (`OP_BUFFER_MAX_SIZE` 4096); 502 lists overflowed PSRAM and boot-looped (StoreProhibited at 0x4000 in `alloc_list`). Shrinking it to 64 fixed it with an identical picture.
- Stock TinyGL does software double maths in lighting, normalising, matrices (`__muldf3`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `cos`). Single-precision rewrite (`tools/float_literals.py` plus sqrt/pow/sin/cos/floor to the f versions) took a piece from about 13 to 9 ms. Still about 18 us per triangle.
- Bench: full clear 24.8 ms, full-frame copy with byte swap 22.2 ms, 512-triangle sphere 9.2 ms, 32-triangle cylinder 0.59 ms, big 95k-pixel sphere 37.9 ms. Frame at N pieces is roughly N x 8 ms plus about 47 ms fixed, plus the 32 ms push: far too slow for 500 pieces (Pipes redraws everything each frame).
- CORRECTION: the first probe used independent triangles; real Pipes uses triangle strips (unit_sphere 16x16 = 544 vertices) and 24-facet quad-strip tubes, so each vertex is lit once. With faithful primitives: sphere 3.7 ms, tube 0.43 ms, about 3.7 ms per piece (2.8 fps at 80 pieces, 1.2 fps at 210). Real Pipes builds spheres via glVertexPointer/glDrawArrays, which TinyGL display lists may record differently (untested risk).
- Wireframe (`*wireframe: True`: no lighting, 5-facet line-strip tubes, line-strip spheres with 4 vertices per slice) is NOT faster: same frame time as solid. Per-vertex overhead is about 4 us (about 1000 cycles) before lighting, which adds only about 2.8 us; the wire sphere has twice the vertices.
- Low-poly (8x8 sphere): 2.3 ms per piece with independent triangles; same cost per triangle (18 us).
- Rod reported a white screen with nothing visible while the log showed a correct canvas (black corner, coloured centre, no white pixels). Cause unknown at time of writing.

Gears works on the device (2026-10-09/10, commit 2115083 on `worktree-spike-tinygl`, committed locally, NOT yet pushed; Rod loved it):

- Unmodified `gears.c` plus helpers (`involute`, `tube`, `normals`, `rotator`, `gltrackball`, `trackball`, `quaternion`) built by wrappers `firmware/src/hacks/gears_gl.c` and `gl_helper_*.c` (include straight from `vendor/`, `USE_GL` per file, never `HAVE_GL` because it changes `ModeInfo` layout). GL layer in `firmware/src/glshim/` (zero-copy into the canvas with `TGL_SWAP_PIXELS`).
- TinyGL incompatibilities found: display list name 0 is handed out first (hacks abort on `!glGenLists(1)`; fixed by starting at 1); vertex arrays count stride in floats and are read at list replay (shim reroutes the six array calls and expands `glDrawArrays` immediately); `glTexGeni`, `glFog*`, `glInterleavedArrays` missing; `memory.c`, `specbuf_get_buffer` prototype and `memset_s` upstream bugs.
- Speed: heavy fixed-seed scene (17.7k vertices per frame) 4 to 5 fps, light scenes about 9 fps. Per frame: clear 24.6 ms, fill about 40 ms, vertex/triangle setup about 100 to 120 ms (about 6 us per vertex), push 32 ms. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables each changed nothing; global `-O2` ICEs on `braid_single.c`. Unexplored levers: triangle setup maths (software float divides), a second core, preferring lighter Gears layouts via overrides.
- Host dump raw files are already un-swapped (`dump_main.c`); `rgb565_to_png.py` reads them as plain RGB565. A script that swaps again shows psychedelic stripes.
- Harness: in a worktree session, commands must be plain (no heredocs, `$VAR`, or complex constructs); `Edit` must use the worktree path, not the shared checkout path.

Landing Gears (Rod approved, 2026-10-10): tracking issue #42, branch `feature/42-gears-gl` (worktree `.claude/worktrees/gears-gl`, based on origin/main 1fa1177). Spike branch `worktree-spike-tinygl` is pushed (2115083). Follow-up issues: #43 TinyGL speed, #44 Pipes, #45 next GL hacks, #46 Flying Toasters, #41 xlockmore docs. Spec `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-09-gears-gl-design.md` committed (8571f29) on the feature branch and awaiting Rod's review; next step is writing-plans, then TDD. Planning artifacts are not to be merged to main. Rod's decisions: pristine TinyGL copy plus build-time patch; land Gears with its random layouts; Rod granted reflash permission for the Gears work.

Shell gotcha: never `cd` into `vendor/` (a symlink to the main checkout) in a worktree session; the shell gets stuck outside the worktree and `ExitWorktree keep` plus `EnterWorktree path=` is needed to recover.

Related: [[project-xlockmore-docs-stale]].

Pipes on TinyGL: too slow as written, and what would change that
Pipes was the first GL hack tried and it is not viable on TinyGL as written.
Record what was learned and what would change that. Depends on #42; see also
#43. Data is in `docs/tinygl-spike.md` on branch `worktree-spike-tinygl`.

## Why it is slow

Pipes does not accumulate. Every frame it clears and redraws every piece so
far from display lists (`draw_pipes` loops over `system_index`), up to about
500 pieces per system with the defaults, under a slowly rotating camera. Cost
grows with the pipe, and every frame changes completely, so pushing only the
changed rows saves nothing.

With Pipes' real primitives (triangle-strip spheres of 16 by 16, 24-facet
quad-strip tubes), measured on the S3 at 464 by 464:

- 3.7 ms per piece, plus about 80 ms fixed per frame.
- 2.8 fps at 80 pieces, 1.2 fps at 210, under 1 fps by 250.
- Wireframe (`*wireframe: True`) is no faster: the same frame times, because
  the cost is per vertex and the wire sphere sends twice the vertices.
- 8 by 8 spheres (about 3.7 times fewer triangles) gave 5.2 fps at 50 pieces,
  3.4 at 100. Not enough on its own.

## What would change that

- Stop redrawing the settled scene. The camera turns only 0.02 degrees per
  frame, so drawing just the newest piece onto the existing frame, and
  redrawing everything only now and then, would make the cost per frame
  constant. Needs interception at the GL layer and slightly changes the look
  (the older pieces lag the camera).
- Faster vertex setup in TinyGL (#43).

## Port notes

- The real spheres come from `unit_sphere` in `sphere.c`, which builds
  `glVertexPointer` arrays and calls `glDrawArrays` inside a display list.
  TinyGL gets that wrong; the array shim from #42 fixes it.
- Pipes also needs `buildlwo.c`, `teapot.c` (built unconditionally),
  `sphere.c`, `gltrackball.c` and `rotator.c`. All are in `hacks/glx/`, so
  they can be copied byte-identical.
- Pipes uses two lights' state and a specular material.

### rodbegbie 2026-10-11T08:48:52Z
Overnight update from Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction (the
night of 2026-10-10 to 11). Host only: nothing has been flashed. The lab is
on branch `feature/44-pipes` in `docs/pipes-lab/` (its README has the
commands and the full table). It builds Pipes and its helpers straight from
`vendor/`, so nothing from Pipes is copied into the repo.

## The incremental redraw works, and is exact

`docs/pipes-lab/pipes_incremental.h` wraps Pipes' `glClear`, `glCallList`,
`glNewList`, `glEndList` and `glXSwapBuffers` (macros before the include; the
hack stays byte-identical). When the clear, the modelview and projection
matrices and the lists so far all match last frame, it skips the clear and
those lists and replays only the new ones. Anything else falls back to a real
clear and a full replay. Over 600 frames, every frame hash matched a full
redraw, both with the camera turning and with it fixed.

With `*rotatepipes: False` (fixed camera), steady frames set up about 300 to
380 vertices instead of up to 977,000, and the swap marks about 11 rows
instead of about 365. With the default turning camera every frame is a full
redraw, so the wrapper never skips.

## New blockers the lab found

- **Memory.** Pipes builds every display list of a screen when the screen
  starts. As written (`*cycles: 5`, `*size: 500`, about 2,500 pieces) that is
  about 44 MB of host heap, roughly 22 MB on the board (a list word is 8 bytes
  on the host and 4 on the board), against about 7 MB of free PSRAM.
  `*cycles: 1` with `*size: 100` is about 0.7 MB on the board; `*cycles: 2`
  with `*size: 150` about 2.3 MB.
- **The fade.** A screen ends with 25 frames that shrink the whole picture,
  so each is a full redraw: about 32,000 vertices at `size` 100 (roughly
  0.2 s a frame at #43's costs) and 977,000 as written.
- **Helpers TinyGL cannot run as copied.** `teapot.c` uses GL evaluators
  (`glMap2f`, `glEvalMesh2`); built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` it uses its triangle
  table (`teapot2.h`) instead. `buildlwo.c` draws `GL_POLYGON`, which this
  TinyGL drops, and the extra vertices overwrote the GL context (a crash on
  frame 16). The lab maps `GL_POLYGON` to `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` for that file only.
  A general guard against the overwrite is on
  `fix/tinygl-unhandled-primitive`.
- **Licences.** `buildlwo.c`, `buildlwo.h`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` carry
  no licence text. The repo's precedent (Pacman's sprites, XMatrix's glyphs)
  is to read such files from `vendor/` at build time and never commit them.

## Decisions for Rod before a real port

1. A fixed camera (`*rotatepipes: False`): that is what makes the
   incremental redraw work.
1. Smaller screens (`*cycles: 1`, `*size: 100` to `200`), to fit PSRAM.
1. The fade: keep it (about 5 s of slow frames per screen at `size` 100), or
   end each screen without it, which the wrapper could do.
1. Build `buildlwo.c`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` from `vendor/` at build
   time, as the sprites are.

With those, steady frames would be a few milliseconds of GL work plus an
11-row push, so Pipes should run at the speed its own 10 ms pause allows.
That is an estimate; nothing has been measured on the board.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/port-hack

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |

    '*rotatepipes: False'

  the lists so far match last frame, the canvas and z-buffer already hold
  them, so the wrapper skips the clear and those lists and replays only the
  new one. Anything else falls back to a real clear and a full replay.

54	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.

56	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
57	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
58	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type

60	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the

64	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the

66	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
67	  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame

70	  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a

73	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines

76	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:

79	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
80	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.

83	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
84	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
85	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
86	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
87	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
88	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in

90	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
91	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
92	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
93	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
94	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
95	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
96	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
97	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
98	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
99	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
100	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
101	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
102	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
103	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
104	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
105	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
106	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
107	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
108	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
109	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:

112	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
113	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
114	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
115	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
116	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
117	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
118	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
119	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a

121	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`

131	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
132	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
133	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
134	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
135	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
136	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
137	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
138	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
139	  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
140	- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,

144	  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
145	  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
146	- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
147	  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
148	  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
149	  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
150	  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
151	  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
152	- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
153	  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
154	  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
155	  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and

157	- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
158	  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
159	  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
160	  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
161	  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
162	  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
163	  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding

167	- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
168	  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel

173	  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it

176	  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
177	  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
178	  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
179	  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.

181	  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
182	- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
183	  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were

185	  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
186	- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same

188	  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed

191	  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
192	  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.

194	  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
195	  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
196	  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables

201	  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since

212	  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
